Synthetic MRI from radiotherapy planning CT images for Head-and-Neck Cancer
Prabhakar Ramachandran1,2,3 Akshay C Dhargave1 Catherine Jones1 Dionee Liefman1 Lachlan McDowell1 Howard Liu1
1Department of Radiation Oncology,Princess Alexandra Hospital,Woolloongabba, Queensland,Australia

3School of Chemistry and Physics, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane,Queensland,Australia

Abstract
Background: Computed Tomography (CT) provides geometric accuracy and

electron density information essential for radiotherapy planning; however, it offers limited soft-tissue contrast.Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) improves tumor visualization but introduces registration uncertainties when acquired separately from the radiotherapy planning CT (pCT).Cross-modality image syn- thesis enables the generation of synthetic MRI (sMRI) directly from pCT and may combine the strengths of both modalities,reducing reliance on MRI access. Purpose: We propose a two-stage deep-learning framework for generat- ing sMRI from pCT image-sets speciﬁcally in head-and-neck (H&N) cancers, providing soft-tissue contrast comparable to ground-truth MR images (gtMRI). Methods: This study included 60 patient cases with H&N cancer treated with radical radiotherapy between March 2022 and April 2024 for model development (50 for training, 10 for validation), plus 10 additional cases, independent of the development cohort for testing.All patients underwent a standard,non-contrast pCT scan followed by an MRI acquired on a 3T Siemens MR simulator.Images were deformably-registered, yielding 10,000 matched CT–MRI slice-pairs for model training.The proposed model utilizes a two-stage architecture,a Pix2Pix conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) for coarse sMRI synthesis, followed by a conditional diffusion model for reﬁnement. To test the model’s robustness, 10 patient cases with both pCT and contrast-enhanced CT (ceCT) were used to generate sMRI.Model performance was assessed using structural similarity index (SSIM),multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM),mean absolute error (MAE), and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). In addition, the geometric agreement of the primary (GTVp_70) and nodal (GTVn_70) gross tumor volumes delineated on sMRI vs. gtMRI was independently assessed by two radiation oncologists (ROs) using the Dice similarity coefﬁcient (DSC),95th- percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95),and average symmetric surface distance (ASSD).

Results: The average MS-SSIM,SSIM,MAE and PSNR for pCT-derived sMRI were 0.82 ± 0.02, 0.70 ± 0.03, 0.05 ± 0.01, and 20.42 ± 0.66 dB, respectively. The mean MS-SSIM and SSIM values for ceCT-derived sMRI were 0.02 lower than those for the corresponding pCT-to-sMRI metrics. For the contour-based evaluation,sMRI-derived GTV contours achieved a mean DSC of 0.56 and 0.60 for GTVp_70, and 0.72 and 0.74 for GTVn_70 across the two ROs, relative to gtMRI contours.

Conclusion: Our proof-of-concept study demonstrates the feasibility of pCT- derived sMRI for H&N cancers using a deep-learning framework. The model produces grayscale patterns and soft-tissue contrast that closely resemble the gtMRI.
KEYWORDS
deep-learning, Head-and-Neck Cancer, image translation, Pix2PixGAN, radiotherapy planning, Synthetic MRI
INTRODUCTION

Head-and-neck (H&N) cancers represent a group of tumors originating in the oral cavity, oropharynx, lar- ynx, hypopharynx, nasopharynx, salivary glands and sinonasal region.1 Radiotherapy is a standard treat- ment modality for these cancers. Gross tumor volumes (GTVs) require manual delineation to prescribe high- dose radiotherapy. Computed tomography (CT) serves as the principal modality for radiotherapy planning, as it provides the essential electron density data required for dose computation.2 Nevertheless,CT has limitations in soft-tissue contrast, and this may impact the accu- rate deﬁnition of tumors and adjacent organs-at-risk (OARs).3 Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides superior soft-tissue contrast, which assists radiation oncologists (ROs) in deﬁning the extent of both primary and nodal GTVs in H&N cancer.4 The absence of elec- tron density information,however,restricts the direct use of MRI datasets for radiotherapy treatment planning, as this information is essential for dose calculation in heterogeneous tissue densities.5

Co-registering MRI to deﬁne tumor extent in radio- therapy planning can lead to target volume alterations classiﬁed as major in over 50% of cases.6 Typically, MRI scans are acquired at different times and under slightly different patient positions; therefore, the co- registration process can introduce errors related to tem- poral changes, anatomical shifts and patient motion.7,8 Furthermore, MRI is not always readily available due to resource constraints or patient contraindications,and its quality can degrade as a result of variations in acqui- sition time and motion artifacts.9 Cross-modality image translation is becoming increasingly popular in radiation oncology as it could help streamline clinical workﬂows and minimize some of the long-standing problems with imaging, contouring, and treatment planning. In the last few years, deep-learning techniques have revolution- ized imaging in radiation oncology,leading to signiﬁcant improvements in image quality and the generation of synthetic images for clinical use.For example,they have led to the generation of synthetic CT from MRI, mainly for the brain and pelvis,10,11 with reduced artifacts, improved Hounsﬁeld unit (HU) values, reduced noise, and the ability to generate synthetic CT from cone-beam CT (CBCT) images for adaptive radiotherapy.12 Similar
progress has been made in translating between Positron

Emission Tomography and CT domains, with the goal of reducing reliance on multi-modality image acquisi- tion and minimizing the registration errors that can arise when images are acquired at different times and under different patient conditions.13 The concept of generating synthetic MRI (sMRI) directly from radiotherapy planning CT (pCT) is appealing,as sMRI enables utilizing a single imaging modality (e.g.,CT) for treatment planning while preserving soft-tissue contrast similar to MRI for OAR and GTV deﬁnition. This would minimize the need for separate patient appointments, reduce reliance on co- registration between separately acquired images, and improve the patient experience by avoiding lengthy MRI acquisition times.14

Several deep-learning architectures have been inves- tigated to date for cross-modality translation. U-Nets play a key role in image synthesis, thanks to their encoder-decoder design and skip connections, which capture both global context and precise anatomical details.15 Generative adversarial networks (GANs) intro- duced the concept of using a generator and discrim- inator to produce realistic images.16 Several studies have utilized GANs for cross-modality synthesis and have shown that they can generate CT-like images from MRI and CBCT images.17,18 GANs mainly rely on paired images for training,which poses a limitation when paired images are not available. This was overcome by the introduction of cycle-consistent GANs (cycle- GANs), which enabled translation between unpaired image domains and have since become a popular approach for MR-to-CT synthesis. However, cycleGANs are likely to introduce hallucinated features or geometric distortions as these architectures do not force geomet- ric ﬁdelity.19 Of late, diffusion models have emerged as a strong alternative to GANs. These models tend to gradually recreate images by denoising the intro- duced noise using a trained noise schedule. Studies have demonstrated their ability to generate high-ﬁdelity medical images.20,21 Their application across medical imaging tasks, including cross-modality synthesis, has been reviewed extensively.22,23

In this proof-of-concept study, we propose a two- stage deep-learning model that utilizes a Pix2Pix- based conditional GAN (Pix2PixGAN) in Stage-1 and a diffusion-based reﬁnement in Stage-2 to transform pCT image-sets into sMRI that closely mimics the ground-truth MRI (gtMRI). This is one of the ﬁrst stud-

ies to explore sMRI in H&N cancers. This technology may assist resource-limited centers to utilize their pCT images to generate sMRI.
2 MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1 Study design and patient cohort

This retrospective study included imaging data from 70 patient-cases with histologically conﬁrmed H&N cancer treated with curative-intent radiotherapy, with or with- out concurrent chemotherapy,between March 2022 and April 2024. Model development used a cohort of 60 patient-cases, randomly split at the patient level training (n = 50) and validation (n = 10) sets using a ﬁxed random seed (42).An additional 10 patient-cases,inde- pendent of the development cohort, were used as the test-cohort. Ethical approval to conduct this study was received from our institutional Human Research Ethics Committee.Written informed consent for the use of data for research was obtained from all patients included in this study. Table 1 summarizes patient and tumor characteristics of the 70-patient study-cohort. The 10 test-cases were held out entirely from model develop- ment and were not used for hyperparameter selection or architectural decisions. Patients with dental implants were also included to ensure the model’s suitability across a broad range of routine clinical cases. into
Imaging acquisition parameters

CT images were acquired on one of two departmen- tal scanners: a Philips® Brilliance™ Big Bore CT or a Toshiba® Aquilion™ Large Bore. Matched acquisition parameters included: 120 kVp, 2 mm slice thickness, 700 mm extended reconstruction ﬁeld-of-view (FOV), with in-plane pixel spacing of 1.367 × 1.367 mm and matrix size of 512 × 512.Reconstruction was performed using each vendor’s default soft-tissue convolution ker- nel (Philips®: kernel B; Toshiba®: FC13). Each patient underwent a pCT scan followed by MRI within our radiotherapy department using a 3-Tesla Siemens® MAGNETOM® Vida MR simulator. Axial 3D Gadolinium (Gadovist® 1.0)-enhanced, T1‑weighted Dixon gtMRI sequences were acquired with 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 mm voxels (TE1 1.58 ms, TE2 2.83 ms, TR 4.66 ms, ﬂip angle 10◦) and consisted of 200 axial slices for each case. During both CT and MRI acquisitions, patients were immobi- lized using a treatment mask attached to a ﬂat tabletop placed over the spine array coil.Two UltraFlex Large 18 coils were positioned superiorly, and two Body 18 coils were positioned over the inferior part of the FOV.
The model was trained exclusively on pCT images, reﬂecting the intended clinical use case. To assess

model robustness and generalizability,we also included contrast-enhanced CT (ceCT) images, acquired at the same imaging session as pCT, in the test-cohort. This enabled us to assess the model’s robustness to vari- ations in image contrast and observe any discernible differences in the generated sMRI.
2.3 Image registration and quality assurance

The pCT images were aligned onto gtMRI using Velocity™ v4.1. Manual rigid alignment was performed to establish a reference, followed by automated rigid (RIR) and deformable registration (DIR) using mutual information-based similarity metrics. To ensure spatial correspondence between modalities,these deformably- registered pCT images were resampled in Velocity™ to match the gtMRI matrix size (256 × 288) and voxel spac- ing (0.9375 × 0.9375 mm). Resampled pCT and gtMRI slices were then paired, yielding 10,000 matched CT– MRI slice-pairs for model development,with resampling ensuring a common spatial resolution across the cohort. To quantify the accuracy of the CT–MRI DIR used to generate the paired training dataset, a landmark-based target registration error (TRE) analysis was performed for all cases using 3D Slicer v5.2.2.24 Four anatomical landmarks clearly identiﬁable on both CT and MRI were selected per patient:the tip of the odontoid process (C2 dens), the basion (anterior foramen magnum), and the anterior-inferior vertebral body corners of C3 and C5. These landmarks were chosen as they represent bony structures with high conspicuity on both modalities and span the craniocaudal extent of the H&N planning vol- ume,thereby providing a representative sampling of the registration ﬁeld. For each patient, corresponding land- mark coordinates were placed independently on gtMRI and resampled pCT volumes. The 3D Euclidean TRE was computed for each landmark pair as:
TRE = Δx2 + Δy2 + Δz2

where Δx, Δy, and Δz are the co-ordinate differences between the resampled pCT and gtMRI landmark posi- tions in the left-right, anteroposterior, and craniocaudal directions, respectively. A per-patient mean TRE was derived by averaging across the four landmarks, and summary statistics were computed across all patients.

Prior to training, matched CT–MRI slice-pairs’ inten- sities were normalized using percentile-based clipping (1st–99th percentile) and linearly rescaled to [0, 1] per- image using min-max normalization. This approach robustly handles outlier intensities arising from den- tal artifacts and air regions without requiring manual windowing.

2.4 Model development: data pre-processing and training

We used a two-stage CT-to-MRI synthesis framework to train our model, as schematically illustrated in Figure 1. In Stage-1,Pix2PixGAN,25 consisting of a generator and a discriminator,was used to generate coarse sMRI from resampled pCT. The generator housed a 2D encoder- decoder U-Net architecture15 with skip connections, convolutional down-sampling, bilinear up-sampling fol- lowed by Conv2D reﬁnement,BatchNorm2D,and ReLU activations.A 70 × 70 PatchGAN discriminator classiﬁed local image-patches as real or synthetic, and provided adversarial feedback to guide generator training. The generator was optimized using a composite objective comprising adversarial loss,16 L1 reconstruction loss, VGG perceptual loss,26 and gradient consistency loss,27 promoting image ﬁdelity,soft-tissue texture preservation, and sharper anatomical boundaries, respectively. Train-

ing used the Adam optimizer28 with batch size = 4, learning-rate = 2 × 10−4, β1 = 0.5, and β2 = 0.999. To prevent data leakage,29 training and validation sets were partitioned at the patient-level. The validation subset monitored convergence,with mean square error (MSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and structural simi- larity index (SSIM) computed after every epoch. Early stopping and learning-rate reduction on plateau were based on validation MSE. Stage-1 was trained for a maximum of 200 epochs with a patience of 30. The checkpoint with the lowest validation MSE was selected for subsequent Stage-2 training.

In Stage-2, the coarse sMRI estimates generated by the pre-trained Pix2PixGAN were then fed into a con- ditional diffusion model. The diffusion reﬁner housed a U-Net backbone with residual blocks, GroupNorm,30 SiLU activation,31 skip connections,and a self-attention bottleneck.32 At every diffusion training time-step t, the U-Net reﬁner received a three-channel input composed

Before diffusion training, the normalized MRI was fur- ther rescaled from [0, 1] to [−1, 1], as standard practice for denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs). Gaussian noise was progressively added over t = 1000 training time-steps using a linear beta schedule ranging from β1 = 1 × 10−4 to βt = 0.02. The model was trained to predict the added Gaussian noise using a mean square error (MSE) denoising objective.33 Training was optimized using AdamW,34 with batch size = 4,learning- rate = 1 × 10−4, weight decay = 0.01, and gradient norm clipping at 1.0. Stage-2 was trained for a maxi- mum of 100 epochs with an early-stopping patience of 15.The checkpoint achieving the lowest validation MSE was retained for subsequent evaluation.

During inference, the reverse diffusion process was initialized by adding partial noise to the Stage-1 coarse sMRI at t = 100 (10% of the full diffusion chain), rather than initializing the process from pure Gaussian noise. The resampled pCT and Stage-1 coarse sMRI remained ﬁxed as conditioning inputs, while the noisy image estimate was iteratively denoised using 50 ances- tral DDPM sampling steps to produce the ﬁnal sMRI. Initializing reﬁnement from a partially noised Stage- 1 estimate constrained the generative search space, thereby reducing inference time and limiting the poten- tial for anatomically implausible image generation. No data augmentation was applied during either training stage;the 10,000 matched CT−MRI slice-pairs provided sufﬁcient anatomical diversity across imaging levels, patient positioning variations,and dental artifact presen-
tations. Training was performed on an NVIDIA® RTX™ A4500 GPU (16 GB GDDR6),with an inference time for the full two-stage pipeline of approximately 3–5 minutes per CT volume.
2.5 Model evaluation

Prior to metric computation, both gtMRI and sMRI were intensity-normalized to [0, 1] per image and histogram matching was applied to the sMRI using gtMRI as the reference to remove residual global intensity scale differ- ences. These generated sMRI were then quantitatively evaluated against the gtMRI using standard image- translation ﬁdelity metrics: SSIM,35 multi-scale SSIM (MS-SSIM),36 mean absolute error (MAE),19 and PSNR. All metrics were computed within the patient body region only, with background air outside the scanned volume excluded using CT-based intensity threshold- ing, ensuring that reported values reﬂect performance within clinically relevant anatomy rather than being inﬂu- enced by uninformative background voxels. Given that MAE and PSNR are computed under per-image normal- ization and over different spatial extents, they capture complementary aspects of image ﬁdelity and are best interpreted independently rather than directly compared against each other.
SSIM is widely used in medical image synthesis as it correlates well with human visual perception of structural ﬁdelity and is deﬁned as:

2.6 Ablation study

To quantify the contribution of the diffusion-based reﬁnement stage, an ablation study was performed in which the same 10 test-cases were evaluated using Stage-1 (Pix2PixGAN) output alone, without Stage-2 processing. All four image-ﬁdelity metrics (MS-SSIM, SSIM, MAE, PSNR) were computed for both Stage-1 and the full two-stage pipeline across every test-case, enabling direct quantitative comparison. Statistical sig- niﬁcance of the metric differences was assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test,with p < 0.05 considered to be signiﬁcant.
Contour-based evaluation

To evaluate the clinical utility of the sMRI, contour- based analysis was performed on all ten test-cases using two GTV sub-volumes:the primary GTV at 70 Gy (GTVp_70) and the nodal GTV at 70 Gy (GTVn_70). The gtMRI contours were retrieved from radiotherapy treatment planning DICOM RTSTRUCT ﬁles generated by the treating ROs, with consensus as per our depart- mental guidelines. Before RO review, the gtMRI and the generated sMRI volumes were rescaled from the normalized [0, 1] intensity range to the [0, 255] dis- play range. No histogram matching was applied to the sMRI volumes shown to the ROs. Two evaluating ROs (RO1 and RO2) independently contoured all 10 test- cases on the sMRI. RO1 had originally been involved in delineating the ground-truth volumes for a subset of these cases at the time of treatment, whereas RO2 had no prior involvement with any of the ground-truth contours. 3 RESULTS
Note.The CI of the mean assumes sample means follow a t–distribution with N – 1 = 9 degrees-of-freedom.

Landmark-based TRE analysis performed across all cases using four anatomical landmarks per case (C2 Dens Tip, C3 Vertebra, C5 Vertebra, and Basion) across the cohort revealed that the mean TRE was 2.15 ± 1.19 mm (median 1.95 mm, IQR 1.14–3.00 mm; range 0.33–4.94 mm). The minimum per-case mean TRE was 1.61 mm,and the maximum was 2.98 mm.

The proposed model generated sMRI volumes with tissue contrast and anatomical detail that closely resem- bled the gtMRI. Figure 2 illustrates pCT-derived sMRI with improved soft tissue contrast relative to pCT for a representative test-case slice, clearly visualizing muscles,fat and submandibular glands.Figure 3 demon- strates that the model preserves anatomical geometry and soft-tissue boundaries across axial levels from the nasal septum through the supraclavicular fossa.
Quantitative performance across the 10 test-cases is shown in Table 2.The model achieved a mean MS-SSIM of 0.82 ± 0.02 (95% CI [0.81, 0.84]), demonstrating

strong structural correspondence between pCT-derived sMRI and gtMRI. Single-scale SSIM values were lower with a mean of 0.70 ± 0.03 (95% CI [0.68, 0.72]), pri- marily due to limited MRI FOV at inferior anatomical levels,typically below supraclavicular slices.Mean MAE was 0.05 ± 0.01 (95% CI [0.04, 0.06]), indicating rel- atively small voxel-wise intensity differences between sMRI and gtMRI. The corresponding PSNR averaged 20.42 ± 0.66 dB (95% CI [19.94, 20.89]), indicating stable reconstruction ﬁdelity across the cohort.

The ablation study comparing Stage-1 (Pix2PixGAN alone) against the full two-stage pipeline across matched slices from all 10 patients demonstrated sta- tistically signiﬁcant improvement attributable to the diffusion-based reﬁnement stage. 4 DISCUSSION

This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that a two- stage Pix2PixGAN–diffusion framework can generate sMRI in close agreement with the gtMRI in patients with H&N cancer. The CT images were acquired on

two in-house scanners (Philips® Brilliance™ Big Bore, and Toshiba® Aquilion™ Large Bore) with matched acquisition parameters (120 kVp, 2 mm slice thick- ness, 1.367 × 1.367 mm native in-plane pixel spacing). The deliberate inclusion of multi-vendor scanners was intended to enhance model robustness and gener- alizability within our departmental workﬂow. As CT is a quantitative imaging modality with standardized HU calibration, inter-vendor intensity differences are expected to be minimal when acquisition parameters are matched.This dual-scanner training strategy reﬂects realistic clinical deployment conditions at our institu- tion, representing a strength of the proof-of-concept design rather than a confound requiring sub-group

The goal of the synthesis framework was to investigate whether MRI-like soft-tissue contrast and enhancement-related appearances could be synthesized directly from pCT, without requiring ceCT as an input. Although pCT does not directly encode contrast-enhancement physiology, the model may learn statistical associations between CT-visible anatomy and the corresponding appearance on gadolinium-enhanced gtMRI. Therefore, the gener- ated sMRI should not be interpreted as an exact or phys- iologically accurate representation of patient-speciﬁc enhancement.

A key methodological concern in studies that rely on CT–MRI DIR for paired data generation is the qual- ity of that registration. Landmark-based TRE analysis across all cases yielded a mean TRE of 2.15 ± 1.19 mm (median 1.95 mm), consistent with literature values of 1 – 3 mm for H&N CT–MRI registration.37 Larger errors were observed at the basion and C3 verte- bra landmarks in cases with greater patient motion, dental artifacts, or susceptibility-related MR distortions, consistent with previously reported challenges in H&N CT–MRI registration.7,8 The CT–MRI DIR was used to create the paired training dataset and, for this study, to bring the sMRI and corresponding gtMRI into the common spatial framework for voxel-wise evaluation.In clinical deployment, however, the model requires only a single pCT image-set as input. Any resampling to the model’s expected input resolution is performed automat- ically as part of the standard pre-processing workﬂow, without registration to a separate reference image, as no gtMRI will be available at the time of use.

The use of a diffusion-based reﬁnement stage to suppress GAN hallucinations is consistent with emerg- ing literature.19 Early stopping in the reverse diffusion process, implemented here via t = 100/1000 initial- ization, has been shown to reduce hallucinations in medical image reconstruction by constraining the gen- erative search space to a neighborhood around the conditional model estimate.38 This principle underlies recently published frameworks such as DynamicDPS,39 which demonstrated that initializing diffusion reﬁnement from a conditional model prediction rather than pure Gaussian noise effectively reduces hallucinations while minimizing computational overhead.Furthermore,GAN- based cross-modality synthesis has been speciﬁcally shown to produce larger reconstruction residuals at tis- sue boundaries,40 the precise regions where our learned residual maps demonstrate the greatest Stage-2 correc- tions,supporting the complementary role of the diffusion reﬁner in addressing known GAN limitations in H&N synthesis.41

The model produced a median MS-SSIM of approx- imately 0.83 (mean 0.82 ± 0.02) and a median SSIM of approximately 0.71 (mean 0.70 ± 0.03), indicating that the sMRI captures a substantial amount of struc- tural detail and broad soft-tissue contrast present in the gtMRI. However, some differences are expected in low-contrast areas and in slices affected by arti- facts.Current literature is heavily focused on MRI-to-CT (sCT) synthesis, and, to date, there are no emerging data on CT-to-MRI synthesis for H&N cancers specif- ically. A study by Li et al.42 employed a conditional GAN to generate sMRI from brain CT scans, yielding an SSIM of 0.94 and PSNR values of nearly 32 dB.

Given that the brain’s structure is far more homoge- neous than that of the H&N, and that diagnostic MRI typically beneﬁts from higher SNR and less geometric distortion, their better performance is expected. In con- trast, our study focuses on H&N radiotherapy planning datasets, which pose challenges due to positional vari- ation,dental artifacts,greater anatomical heterogeneity, susceptibility-related distortions,geometric inconsisten- cies, and disease extent that varies between patients. A lumbar-spine CT-to-MRI cycleGAN model achieved mean SSIM values as low as 0.28 and PSNR around 12 dB on its validation set,43 highlighting the difﬁculty of obtaining MRI-like contrast when both structure and intensity change substantially. Douglass et al.44 utilized Pix2Pix to generate cranial sMRI from optical surface images, achieving an MS-SSIM of 0.83. Their input method differs substantially from CT; yet their results indicate that MS-SSIM values above ∼0.8 demon- strate strong cross-modality performance in challenging anatomical contexts.More broadly,cross-modality med- ical image translation studies typically report SSIM values between 0.75 and 0.90 and PSNR values between 18 and 30 dB, though these values are highly dependent on anatomy, acquisition quality, and model architecture.45 Our results fall well within this published range. We also observed a relatively small difference between the mean and median scores for all four param- eters: MS-SSIM, SSIM, PSNR, and MAE, suggesting consistent model behavior across most slices.However, some outliers with low MS-SSIM and SSIM values were observed,primarily in inferior neck slices and the shoul- der region, as well as in slices affected by swallowing motion or dental artifacts. An MAE of ∼4 – 5% of the normalized intensity scale indicates that the generated sMRI replicates MRI signal intensities with reasonable ﬁdelity. While our model was trained exclusively using pCT images,we also tested its performance on both pCT and ceCT image-sets. For ceCT-derived sMRI, PSNR decreased marginally, while MAE increased slightly. A closer examination of Figure 6 reveals that pCT-derived sMRI has the potential to effectively highlight nodal volumes.

From a clinical perspective, it is encouraging that high SSIM and MS-SSIM values were consistently observed in the oropharyngeal region,where GTVs and OARs are routinely contoured. Figure 3 shows that sMRI reproduces some of the key anatomical struc- tures, such as mucosal surfaces, parotid glands, and the spinal cord, more clearly than CT alone, demon- strating promise for potential clinical applications. First, sMRI could assist centers with limited access to MR simulation by providing pseudo-MR contrasts from pCT scans.Second,it may reduce the need for separate diag- nostic or planning MR appointments. Third, sMRI could be integrated into the auto-segmentation workﬂow to enhance the delineation of GTVs, with appropriate RO oversight.46

An exploratory scanner-vendor comparison showed a small observed difference in MS-SSIM (Philips® 0.82 ± 0.06 vs.Toshiba® 0.82 ± 0.07;difference 0.002), as detailed in the Results. However, given the small per-vendor sample sizes, this should not be taken as evidence of multi-vendor generalizability,which requires formal evaluation in the planned multi-center validation phase.
The contour-based analysis provides an initial clin-

ical validation of the sMRI for GTV delineation. The GTVp_70 DSC (0.56 and 0.60) across the two eval- uating ROs is lower than that of GTVn_70 (0.72 and 0.74), consistent with the inherently more challenging nature of primary tumor contouring due to irregular mar- gins and mucosal involvement. The GTVn_70 DSC is broadly comparable to published inter-observer vari- ability data for H&N GTV delineation on MRI, where median DSC values of 0.73 – 0.76 for nodal volumes have been reported across experienced multi-observer studies.47,48 These studies consistently note that nodal volumes exhibit better inter-observer agreement than primary tumors owing to clearer capsular boundaries. Our reported GTVp_70 DSC aligns with primary GTV segmentation benchmarks on MRI.47 The observed under-segmentation tendency for GTVp_70 may reﬂect limitations in sMRI soft tissue contrast at the primary tumor margin. These results represent an encourag- ing preliminary step;further evaluation with experienced ROs and a larger cohort is warranted. This study did not include a CT-only contouring arm, as CT- and MRI- based GTV delineation are already known to differ substantially, with consensus guidelines recommending MRI for GTVs49,50; the relevant question tested here is whether sMRI approximates true MRI-based delineation when MRI is unavailable.

Despite these encouraging ﬁndings, we acknowl- edge that our study has a few limitations. This initial exploratory proof-of-concept study was restricted to 70 patients from a single institution. A further limitation is that the training and evaluation pCT images had been deformably registered with gtMRI to build matched pairs, so performance on native, unwarped pCT at deploy- ment was not directly tested. The small registration error (mean TRE 2.15 ± 1.19 mm) indicates accept- able alignment, but validation on native CT remains an important next step. Our present study was limited to 2D slices, primarily to mimic the radiotherapy work- ﬂow, in which these slices are used to reconstruct 3D volumes in the planning system.While image-level met- rics such as SSIM, MS-SSIM, PSNR, and MAE provide valuable global assessments, further clinical evaluation incorporating comprehensive GTV and OAR contour assessment, dose recalculation studies, and reader- based image quality scoring would provide additional insight into the clinical utility of the proposed approach. As this is a proof-of-concept study, thorough vali- dation through multi-center trials, independent clinical

evaluation, and reader-based assessment is required before this framework can be considered for routine clin- ical implementation. A prospective, blinded comparison of CT-only vs. sMRI-assisted delineation is identi- ﬁed as an important direction for future work. Future work will evaluate uncertainty estimation frameworks to propagate registration uncertainty into the synthesis quality assessment.Future studies will additionally focus on out-of-distribution detection and localized failure analysis across anatomical subregions, together with reader-based perceptual scoring, to further establish the clinical robustness of the proposed framework.Fur- ther optimization of this model through multi-institutional and multi-vendor training and testing, followed by inde- pendent validation, would add substantial value to the emerging data in this ﬁeld.The clinical utility of an sMRI solution derived from CT imaging would be far-reaching, alleviating resource constraints in many clinical settings and enhancing the patient experience.
5 CONCLUSION

Our proof-of-concept deep-learning model demon- strates the feasibility of generating sMRI from conven- tional radiotherapy pCT images, with close structural similarity to gtMRI. Landmark-based TRE analysis indi- cated millimeter-level spatial accuracy for the CT–MRI DIR used to align the image-pairs. The proposed approach has the potential to supplement CT by assist- ing with delineation of GTVs for radiotherapy treatment planning and may be particularly valuable for centers that rely solely on CT-based workﬂows.To build on this, further training and validation of the model on larger, multi-center cohorts spanning a wider range of H&N subsites, tumor stages, and scanner protocols are war- ranted to improve robustness and generalizability before clinical adoption.
